To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
GAPDH, HPRT and RPL13A are reliable housekeeping genes for use in QPCR experiments involving HIV and HSV-1 infected cells.
the housekeeping genes GAPDH, ACTB and HPRT1 are suitable normalisers for the majority of the viral infections and cell types tested.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a set of reliable housekeeping genes for use with QPCR in viral infections.

determining the most appropriate housekeeping genes for use with QPCR experiments on cells infected with four human pathogens, namely, Human Immunodeficiency virus type I (HIV), Herpes Simplex virus type 1 (HSV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Varicella zoster Virus (VZV).
the choice of appropriate housekeeping genes for the normalisation of quantitative PCR (QPCR) analysis in the context of four viral infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GAPDH, ACTB, HPRT1, RPLP0 and B2M are the most suitable housekeeping genes to normalise QPCR experiments in the context of HIV and HSV-1 infections.
the most reliable housekeeping genes for QPCR analysis of HIV-1, HSV-1, VZV and CMV infections are: GAPDH and HPRT1 for HIV-1; GAPDH for HSV-1; GAPD and TBP for VZV and GAPD and TATA for CMV.
the most reliable and consistent housekeeping gene for QPCR analysis of cells infected by these viruses was the ribosomal protein S9 (RPS9) gene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most reliable housekeeping genes for use in the normalisation of QPCR experiments are those that are involved in the regulation of cell cycle progression and cell proliferation.
GAPDH is a suitable housekeeping gene for the majority of QPCR experiments involving these viruses.
GAPDH is a reliable normalising gene for QPCR analysis of HIV, HSV-1, CMV and VZV infected cells and is the best normalising gene to use in the context of these viral infections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a single housekeeping gene for all QPCR experiments is not advisable.
the use of a single normaliser for all samples in a QPCR experiment is not always appropriate and that the choice of a normaliser should be made on an experimental basis.
no single housekeeping gene is universally applicable to all viruses and cell types and the choice of housekeeping gene must be made on a case-by-case basis.
